extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, patent practitioners, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evidentiary criteria governing novelty, utility, and the sufficiency of patent specifications, including who may testify and what proof a patentee must produce at trial to support validity and priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as prima facie evidence of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the patentee must swear he is the true inventor before obtaining a patent, the patent is 'prima facie evidence that he has made the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption is rebuttable; prior experimental work by others may still allow a subsequent inventor who perfected the invention to obtain a valid patent. The jury must decide whether prior efforts amounted to completed invention or mere experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of hearsay/about-heard-of evidence on prior completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony that persons 'who make it the business of their lives' to know inventions had heard of the invention prior to the patentee is very strong presumptive evidence that prior experiments had in fact produced the perfected result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such persons had not heard of it, that tends strongly to show prior experiments were incomplete. Testimony that persons had merely heard of an announcement (but not seen the thing) is strong presumptive evidence but is not conclusive without proof the thing was actually made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's declarations as res gestae to fix date
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee may introduce his own declarations describing the nature and objects of the invention as part of the res gestae to establish when the invention was completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations that describe details and explain operations are legitimate evidence to fix origin; mere assertion that he 'invented' at some prior date may be objected to. Such declarations must describe details to be persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of utility required
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must offer some evidence of the utility of his invention; the degree of utility is not material, but it must be capable of some use beneficial to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility is ordinarily proved by testimony of persons conversant with the subject (saying whether the thing is capable of the designed use or an improvement), or by other evidence such as large orders or licenses taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification sufficiency statutory standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must show the specification is 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, as to enable any person, skilled in the art or science to which it appertains, to make, construct, compound, or use the thing patented.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficiency may sometimes be apparent on the face of a simple specification; for complicated inventions, evidence (usually expert) is advisable to show those skilled in the art can apply it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial burden at trial — slight evidence in opening
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight evidence of the sufficiency of the specification offered in opening is generally enough to make it incumbent on the defendant to falsify the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How much evidence should be presented in opening versus reserved for reply depends on trial circumstances, but a small showing suffices initially to shift the burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper witnesses for sufficiency: practical workmen of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The general standard adopts the ability of skilful practical workmen (artisans, operators, manufacturers) of ordinary skill in the relevant branch as the test of a specification's sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the persons to whom the specification is supposed to be addressed; their ability to practise the invention from the specification without invention or addition is the key test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of higher scientific/theoretical witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinct class of witnesses of higher theoretical scientific knowledge who may be competent to testify, but the law generally favors the practical workman standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While both practical and theoretical witnesses may fall within 'skilled in the art', the law treats practical workmen as the primary standard because the specification is directed to those who will apply it in industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-specific tests for different invention types
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the practicality test to the nature of the invention: e.g., for a pump, could a pump-maker of ordinary skill construct it from the plan; for a composition, could a practical chemist make the compound; for a process, would a competent workman produce the effect by following directions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard of skill will vary with the subject matter; the question is always whether a person of ordinary skill in that branch could carry the invention into effect from the directions given, without further invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable without requiring invention by workmen
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable competent workmen to practise the invention 'without invention or addition of their own' and must not merely set them a problem to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is improper to frame a specification that requires persons to 'set themselves a problem to solve' or to tax their ingenuity; the specification should supply the way of doing the thing, not just suggest it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose best mode and particular expedients known
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee is acquainted with any particular mode by which the invention may most conveniently be carried into effect, he ought to state it in his specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose known facilitating details (e.g., use of tallow in a process) can render the specification bad; the patentee is bound to a bona fide and candid disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must not cast expense and labor of experiments on the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must 'actually and plainly set forth what the invention is, and how it is to be carried into effect,' so as to save the public the trouble of making experiments and trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'will be easily learned by experience' are insufficient; a specification that leaves essential details to be discovered by trial is bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings are illustrative not limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: A drawing should be treated as an illustration of the invention, not as confining the invention to the particular angle or dimensions shown in the drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the drawing were treated as limiting, the invention would be confined to the precise depiction; instead the specification should provide directions enabling construction in other forms or angles when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple inventions in one patent must each be supported
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent contains more than one invention, each must be useful and described in the specification so that people 'clearly' know what each invention is and how to carry it into effect; otherwise the patent fails for those inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party who places multiple inventions in one patent risks invalidation unless each invention is separately supported by the specification and is useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of adequate dimensions/data when essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Where practical construction turns on particular measurements (e.g., length of rods, position of eccentric axis), absence of necessary dimensions or means to find them may render the specification insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable data (such as wheel diameter and immersion) may be fair to require; if essential parameters cannot be ascertained except by subsequent experiments, the specification may be bad. Evidence from skilled witnesses as to whether reasonable data suffice is material.
